5392.text: Mic 6:8 renders darash as 'require' (what does the Lord require) rather than the more common 'seek' — a divergence in surface form emphasizing God as the DEMANDING party rather than the seeker, shifting agency onto God's requirement of covenant ethics from man, distinct from the more typical human-seeking-God direction seen in Hos 10:12 and 1Chr 10:14.

5397.text: In Mic 6:8, darash ('require') co-occurs with M05/M18 (good), M12 (justice), M51 (love), M07/M50 (kindness), M09 (humbly). This characteristic's vantage: darash frames God as the REQUIRING party, making the other M-codes (justice, love-kindness, humility) the CONTENT of what is required — seeking/requiring here functions as the covenantal umbrella-verb under which the triad of ethical characteristics are named.

5401.text: In Mic 6:8, the requiring operation is initiated by the Lord (party, T7) and directed toward 'man' (party, T8) — God as the demanding party toward humanity.

14224.text: Part 2 verses: what they add. Three new strands: (a) The eye wasting, as in Job 17:7; "My eye wastes away because of grief; it grows weak because of all my foes" (Psa 6:7), after "every night I flood my bed with tears" (6:6); "My eye is wasted from grief; my soul and my body also. For my life is spent with sorrow" (Psa 31:9–10); The eye is where ka'as shows in the body, in all three texts (Job 17:7; Psa 6:7; 31:9); What turns Psa 6 round is being heard: "the Lord has heard the sound of my weeping. The Lord has heard my plea" (6:8–9). In Psa 10:14, "you do see, for you note mischief and vexation, that you may take it into your hands; to you the helpless commits himself". The vexation is seen by God, and the helpless hands it over; (b) Provocation from those closest; "A foolish son is a grief to his father and bitterness to her who bore him" (Pro 17:25); The reverse direction: "Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger" (Eph 6:4), and "do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged" (Col 3:21); Vexation passes both ways between parent and child. Col 3:21 names its outcome as losing heart. Hannah's rival (1Sa 1:6) was a co-wife. These are the family members; (c) Qoheleth's vexation: the vexation of the thinker and the worker; Knowing brings it: "in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow" (Ecc 1:18). This comes after "I applied my heart to know wisdom … this also is but a striving after wind" (1:17); Work brings it, and it keeps the heart awake: "his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest" (2:23); "all his days he eats in darkness in much vexation and sickness and anger" (5:17); Its answer is enjoyment received as God's gift: "There is nothing better … than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God" (2:24), and "this is the gift of God" (5:19); It is to be removed: "Remove vexation from your heart, and put away pain from your body" (11:10), after "Rejoice, O young man … let your heart cheer you" (11:9); It is sometimes better than laughter: "Sorrow [ka'as] is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (7:3). The one place where ka'as is valued. The face is sad and the heart made good. Face and heart go in opposite directions.

15731.text: H5627 (sarah) adds a distinct instigation sense: it names speaking rebellion, inciting others toward covenant abandonment (Deut 13:5's false prophet who taught rebellion; Jer 28:16, 29:32, prophets who uttered or spoke rebellion against the LORD), a verbal-agency variant not present in the other members.

15770.text: na'aph as a finite or infinitive-absolute verb form, narrating a specific act rather than naming a person: a narrated historical event (Jer 29:23, they have committed adultery with their neighbors' wives), an infinitive-absolute generic sin-listing (Hos 4:2, Jer 23:14, Jer 7:9, adultery catalogued alongside swearing, lying, murder, stealing), and Jeremiah's extended covenant-infidelity metaphor (committing adultery with stone and tree, Jer 3:9; they have committed adultery, and blood is on their hands, Ezek 23:37).

15791.text: sarah (H5627, revolt) consistently as a noun naming spoken or taught rebellion against the Lord: a false prophet who taught rebellion (Deut 13:5), prophets who uttered or spoken rebellion (Jer 28:16, 29:32). The verbal-instigation register is distinct from bagad and ma'al's relational-betrayal register: this root names the act of articulating or teaching defection, not merely committing it.

15795.text: apostasia (G0646) at Acts 21:21 renders as the English verb forsake (teach to forsake Moses), but its own morph is N-ASF, a noun, not a verb. The Greek literally reads something like apostasy from Moses; the English surface restructures the noun-phrase into a verb clause, so the word's grammatical shape (an abstract-noun accusation of departure) differs from what the English sentence structure suggests (a direct verbal instruction to abandon).

15798.text: All 5 of sarah's occurrences carry noun morph (HNcfsa) yet 2 of them (Isa 1:5 rebel, Isa 31:6 revolted) render as English verbs, the same noun-rendered-as-verb pattern found for apostasia (G0646, Acts 21:21): two languages, two separately catalogued strongs, the same translation-restructuring move, an abstract Hebrew or Greek noun becoming an English finite verb. Worth checking whether this is a systematic ESV rendering habit for this whole semantic domain (apostasy and rebellion nouns) rather than two isolated cases.

16217.text: 14. Cross-cutting observations for Batch G [Claude reading]: Life is held in the breath and the soul, and it is God's to give and gather.; "Living soul" is shared with the animals. God's breathing is what marks Gen 2:7.; One decision of God's heart could gather every breath back (Job 34:14–15).; In the flood narrative God's heart changes while man's heart does not (Gen 6:5–6 → 8:21).; *rûaḥ* moves across senses within a single passage, and the passage uses the movement: Eze 37: carrying Spirit → breath → winds → "my Spirit within you"; Judg 15: rushing Spirit → one's own spirit returning; Jon 4: an appointed wind that makes the soul wish to die; Strength and hardness are one word. *ḥāzaq* is courage, hardening and the nerve to kill, according to what the heart is set toward (§3.3). This mirrors the tender heart (Batch F §6): neither softness nor strength of heart has a fixed moral value.; Revisit (Batch H §7.4): more words of this kind — *nāṣar* (keep the heart / the "guarded" wily heart), *šāmar*, vengeance, fatness of soul and of heart, *šāgâ*, kinship-flesh.; The inner components give way in order. Samson (Judg 16): the soul vexed; the heart told; the strength gone; the Lord gone; The strength returns only when asked for, and joined to the soul's consent to die.; Jacob (Gen 45): heart numb → spirit revived by words and sight.; The soul is what one swears by and what one bargains for.; Oaths "as your soul lives" mark adherence at a cost (Elisha, the Shunammite, Uriah) or protection with fear (Zedekiah).; Souls are hunted for bread (Eze 13) and "captured" by the wise (Pro 11:30).; Nothing can be given in return for a soul (Mic 6:7–8; Mat 16:26).; Eating and drinking recur at inner thresholds, now in three registers: the merry heart (Batch F §7); the heart sustained by bread before it is made merry (Judg 19:5, 8); the soul that blesses after a meal and wine (Gen 27:25); Also: the sad heart at a feast that turns to prayer (Hannah, Nehemiah), and the wine-threshold refused (Uriah).; Enticement and stirring show how other agents reach the inner seat: God stirs human spirits (Cyrus, Pul, the remnant).; God sends an other-spirit to entice through prophets' mouths (1Ki 22).; God allures and speaks to the heart (Hos 2:14).; Desire, gods and false teachers entice hearts and souls.

16932.text: What the pattern shows [Claude reading]: The merry heart is a threshold state. In every narrative it comes after eating and drinking and immediately before a decisive event, which others usually initiate. The good heart lowers guard. What enters at that moment decides the outcome: murder (Amnon); exposure and anger (Vashti, Ahasuerus); mockery turned to catastrophe (Samson); outrage (Gibeah); approach and redemption (Ruth); a dead heart the next morning (Nabal); God's claim on the soul (the rich fool); The heart's condition swings overnight. Nabal: merry heart → dead heart (1Sa 25:36–37). Ahasuerus: merry heart → burning anger (Est 1:10–12). The heart's state is not stable; wine sets it high, and news or refusal drops it.; 1Ki 21 joins spirit and heart. Ahab's spirit is vexed and he stops eating. Jezebel prescribes food and a good heart, secured by injustice. A spirit-state is "cured" by manufacturing a heart-state — the only place in the batch where one is treated through the other.; Positive merriment exists outside the narratives: "they … went to their homes joyful and glad of heart for all the goodness that the Lord had shown" (1Ki 8:66); "A joyful heart is good medicine" (Pro 17:22); "A glad heart makes a cheerful face" (Pro 15:13); "let your heart cheer you … But know that … God will bring you into judgment" (Ecc 11:9); When the heart is good because of God, no threshold event follows. When it is good from wine, one does.; Revisit (Batch G) — the threshold pattern extended: The step before the merry heart: "Strengthen your heart with a morsel of bread" (Judg 19:5, 8). The father-in-law alternates *strengthen* (5, 8) and *merry* (6, 9). Each round delays departure (G §3.1).; The threshold engineered and refused: David "made him drunk" (2Sa 11:13). Uriah, who had sworn "as your soul lives, I will not do this thing" (11:11), still does not go home. The next morning: the death letter (11:14–15) (G §4).; The soul's version: "prepare for me delicious food … that my soul may bless you" (Gen 27:4). "He ate; and he brought him wine, and he drank" (27:25) → the irreversible blessing of the false firstborn → Esau's hatred "in his heart" (27:41; §8.2 below) (G §13.3).; The Samson sequence in full (Judg 16:15–30): soul vexed (16); heart told (17); strength and the Lord gone (19–20); the Philistines' merry hearts (25); strength asked for (28)

19406.text: Isaiah 65:12 — "chose what I did not delight in": This is an oracle. It opens with God, not with the people: *"I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me … I said, “Here I am, here I am,”"* (v1); *"I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, following their own devices"* (v2); The wrong choosing in v12 is made in front of a God who is calling and holding out his hands.; The oracle shows what they turned to instead: sacrifices *"in gardens"*, sitting *"in tombs"*, eating *"pig’s flesh"* (v3–4); a pride that says *"do not come near me, for I am too holy for you"* (v5); they *"forget my holy mountain"* and *"set a table for Fortune and fill cups of mixed wine for Destiny"* (v11); They put their trust in luck and fate.; The answer turns on their own word: *"I will destine you to the sword"* (v12). In Hebrew, "Destiny" (Meni, H4507) and "destine" (manah, H4487) come from the same root. They poured cups for Destiny, and the Lord destines them. What they chose to trust becomes the form their judgement takes.; The verse then gives the reason, and the reason is in the inner being: *"because, when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen, but you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in."* The choosing does not stand alone. It is the far end of not answering and not listening. When they turned away from the voice calling them, that was already a choice, and choosing what God does not delight in is where it ends.; There is a phrase to set beside Joshua 24. There, the choice turned on what was *"evil in your eyes"*. Here they *"did what was evil in my eyes"*. The measure has moved from their eyes to God's, and his delight is the standard their choice is judged by.; In the same oracle the word "chosen" is used of the others: *"my chosen shall possess it"* (v9); *"You shall leave your name to my chosen for a curse"* (v15); So in one passage there are those who chose what God did not delight in, and those God calls *"my chosen"*. The outcome sets the two side by side and reaches the inner being on both sides: *"my servants shall sing for gladness of heart, but you shall cry out for pain of heart and shall wail for breaking of spirit"* (v14). The choice ends in the heart and spirit of the one who made it.

19855.text: Choosing before a God who has already acted: In these verses the human choice is never the first move.; At Shechem it comes after eleven verses of what the Lord did, beginning with *"I took your father Abraham from beyond the River"* (Jos 24:3).; In Isaiah 65 the wrong choice is made in front of a God who says *"Here I am, here I am"* and *"I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people"* (65:1–2).; At the Jerusalem council the church's choosing follows Peter's word that *"God made a choice among you"* (Act 15:7), in the same verb.

The verse says how the elect were chosen. It does not say why the rest were not.

20287.text: 1 Thessalonians 1:4: "For we know, brothers loved by God, that he has chosen you": Paul writes of what he remembers of them: *"your work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ"* (v3). Then: *"For we know, brothers loved by God, that he has chosen you, because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction"* (v4–5).; "Know" is *oida* (G6063). Here another person knows that someone has been chosen. The ESV joins v4 to v5 with "because": the knowing rests on how the gospel came to them. The passage goes on to what was seen in them: *"you received the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit"* (v6); *"you became an example to all the believers"* (v7); *"your faith in God has gone forth everywhere"* (v8); *"you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven"* (v9–10)

20288.text: What this verse shows of others around the choosing: Another person can know that someone is chosen.; In this verse the knowing rests on what was seen when the gospel came: power, the Holy Spirit and full conviction.; What is seen in the chosen is faith, love and hope (v3), joy in affliction (v6), and turning from idols (v9).; The one who knows it gives thanks and prays for them (v2).

20292.text: 1 Peter 2:6: "a cornerstone chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame": *"For it stands in Scripture: 'Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone, a cornerstone chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame'"* (v6).; The other's inner act here is believing (*pisteuō*, G4100), toward the chosen stone. The outcome is stated: *"will not be put to shame"*.; The next verses divide people by it: *"So the honor is for you who believe, but for those who do not believe, 'The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone,' and 'A stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense.' They stumble because they disobey the word, as they were destined to do"* (v7–8).

20293.text: 2 John 1: "The elder to the elect lady and her children, whom I love in truth": *"The elder to the elect lady and her children, whom I love in truth, and not only I, but also all who know the truth, because of the truth that abides in us and will be with us forever"* (v1–2).; The love is the elder's, and it is shared by *"all who know the truth"*. "Love" is *agapaō* (G0025). "Know" is *ginōskō* (G1097). Both are toward the one called elect. The verse grounds the love *"in truth"* and *"because of the truth that abides in us"*. It does not ground it in the choosing.; The letter goes on: *"I rejoiced greatly to find some of your children walking in the truth"* (v4), and *"this is love, that we walk according to his commandments"* (v6).; The HIB/qualifier file has the relation as "none". The reading agrees that the love is not bound to the choosing. "Elect" names the reader.

20309.text: Job 34:33 — Elihu: "For you must choose, and not I": Elihu's verdict follows anyway: *"Job speaks without knowledge; his words are without insight"*; *"Would that Job were tried to the end"* (v35–36).; The book records what Job did choose, and when. It is not after Elihu, but after the Lord speaks (38–41): *"I have uttered what I did not understand, things too wonderful for me"* (42:3); *"I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you; therefore I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes"* (42:5–6); *"I despise"* is the same verb, H3988A, as Elihu's *"you reject"*. In the record the verb stands without its own tagged object; the ESV supplies *"myself"*. I read this as Elihu having named the right kind of choice, a refusing, but the choice being made when Job's eye saw the Lord, not under Elihu's argument. The text gives the order (*"now my eye sees you; therefore"*). It does not comment on Elihu.

20313.text: The refusing verb returns at the end. Elihu's *"you reject"* and Job's *"I despise … and repent"* are the same verb (34:33; 42:6), the verb of *"refuse the evil"* (Isa 7:15). In Job the choice is made when *"now my eye sees you"* (42:5). This stands beside the test reading of Jos 24, where the people chose from what they had seen.

20538.text: Own devices against God's outstretched hands: "I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, following their own devices" (Isa 65:2).

21056.text: The verb is a demand put as a question: what the Lord asks of Israel (tree H7592 1a1 'to ask, ask for').

21057.text: Fear here is reverent awe before the Lord (tree H3372 1a3 'to fear, reverence, honour, respect').

21058.text: Ways here is the figure for the course of a life lived toward the Lord (tree H1870 1e 'of course of life (fig.)').

21059.text: Love here is love of a person toward God (tree H0157 1a3 'human love for or to God').

21060.text: Serve here is the service of the Lord (tree H5647 1a4 'to serve (God)').

21061.text: Heart and soul together say that the service is given with the whole inner seat (tree H3824 1a2 'heart (of man)'; H5315 1a 'the inner being of man').

21071.text: The one served is the Lord their God.

21075.text: Israel is to walk in the Lord's ways and to love him.

21077.text: The speaker turns to this after recalling forty days on the mountain and the Lord's unwillingness to destroy them (Deu 10:10-11).

21082.text: Israel is to serve the Lord with the whole inner seat.

21083.text: The one question is answered by four infinitives: to fear, to walk, to love and to serve.

21084.text: The four are one requirement, not four separate ones.

21085.text: The question states what the Lord requires; it is not asked to gain information.

21315.text: Called is God's own act of summoning, choosing or appointing a person or people; it bears on their inner response (faith, obedience, hope), which other words of the verse name, and is the outward act upon them.

21319.text: Calling is the standing given by God's call (the vocation); it is what diligence, worthiness or walking is directed at, not an inner operation in itself.

21328.text: Calls is God's own act of summoning, choosing or appointing a person or people; it bears on their inner response (faith, obedience, hope), which other words of the verse name, and is the outward act upon them.

21465.text: Piety is here the godliness, devoutness, reverence or uprightness of a person as a state of the heart toward God or toward what is right (a devout man who feared God, godliness trained and pursued, uprightness of heart, reverence and awe).

21500.text: Uprightness is here the godliness, devoutness, reverence or uprightness of a person as a state of the heart toward God or toward what is right (a devout man who feared God, godliness trained and pursued, uprightness of heart, reverence and awe).
